question: What makes an IV fluid 'isotonic'?

options.A: It draws fluid out of the blood vessels and into the tissue cells
options.B: It contains large protein molecules that cannot cross membranes
options.C: It causes body cells to swell by forcing water inside them
options.D: It has the same particle concentration as blood plasma

explanation: You've got this! Isotonic fluids match the natural concentration of our blood, meaning they safely boost fluid volume without causing water to rush into or out of our cells. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why would a doctor order a hypotonic fluid like 0.45% Normal Saline?

options.A: To maintain a stable vein without altering any fluid balance
options.B: To rapidly replace large volumes of blood loss from trauma
options.C: To treat severe cellular dehydration by moving water into tissues
options.D: To pull excess fluid out of swollen brain cells and tissues

explanation: Think of hypotonic fluids as having fewer particles than blood. When a patient is super dehydrated, these fluids move out of the veins and into thirsty cells to plump them back up! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h1)

question: What is the safest way to check a patient's identity before starting an IV?

options.A: Look at the medication chart resting on the bedside table
options.B: Ask the client what room they are currently staying in
options.C: Check the client's identification band using two unique identifiers
options.D: Call out the client's full name and wait for a head nod

explanation: Safety first! Always use two patient identifiers (like name and hospital number on the ID band) to make sure you are giving the right treatment to the right person. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h2)

question: A patient with heart failure needs an IV infusion. What is your most important pre-infusion check?

options.A: Choosing a vein located in the dominant hand for comfort
options.B: Selecting the largest gauge needle available for rapid infusion
options.C: Warming the intravenous fluid bag to body temperature first
options.D: Listening to the client's lung sounds and checking baseline vital signs

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Heart failure patients struggle to handle extra fluid. Checking their lungs and vitals first gives you a baseline so you can catch early signs of fluid overload. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h2)

question: When inserting a peripheral IV catheter, what angle should your needle enter the skin?
explanation: An angle of 15 to 30 degrees is the sweet spot! It lets you slide right through the skin and gently catch the superficial vein without poking through the back wall. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h3)

question: Why must you let the skin antiseptic dry completely before starting an IV stick?

options.A: To allow the chemical to fully destroy microorganisms on the skin
options.B: To ensure the vein stays plump and easy to palpate
options.C: To prevent the sticky dressing from sliding off wet skin
options.D: To stop the client from feeling a sharp burning sensation

explanation: Patience pays off! Antiseptics like chlorhexidine need a little contact and drying time to actually kill the germs on the skin before you puncture it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h3)

question: What does the 'drop factor' on an IV tubing package tell you?

options.A: The number of drops delivered in one milliliter of fluid
options.B: The maximum speed the fluid can flow through the line
options.C: The total number of milliliters the tubing can hold
options.D: The hours the administration set can remain sterile

explanation: You've got this. Drop factor tells you the size of the drops the tubing makes, which you need to know when calculating manual drip rates (gtt/min). [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h4)

question: An order reads: 1,000 mL normal saline over 8 hours. Your tubing drop factor is 15 gtt/mL. What is the flow rate?
explanation: Math made simple! Multiply total volume (1000) by drop factor (15) to get 15,000 drops, then divide by total minutes (480 mins). That gives you roughly 31 drops per minute. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h4)

question: How often should you change a clean, intact transparent IV dressing?

options.C: Only when the IV line is removed

explanation: Standard hospital guidelines recommend changing transparent peripheral IV dressings every 7 days unless they get dirty, loose, or wet. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h5)

question: Why is it important to regularly check the connection joints of an IV setup?

options.A: To ensure the gravity roller clamp is set to the maximum speed
options.B: To check if the plastic tubing needs to be warmed with a heating pad
options.C: To make sure the manufacturer label matches the client's chart
options.D: To prevent accidental disconnection, fluid leakage, and bacterial entry

explanation: Keeping connections tight keeps the system sterile! It stops messy leaks and prevents nasty bacteria from sneaking into your patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the main difference between infiltration and extravasation?

options.A: Extravasation makes the skin feel very cold, whereas infiltration makes it feel hot
options.B: Infiltration only happens in the legs, while extravasation happens in the arms
options.C: Extravasation involves tissue-damaging vesicant drugs that can cause necrosis
options.D: Infiltration requires immediate surgical removal of the vein tissue

explanation: Both mean fluid leaked out of the vein, but extravasation is extra scary because the leaked drug is a 'vesicant' that can actually destroy the surrounding tissue and cause severe sores. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h6)

question: Your IV patient suddenly feels short of breath, has crackles in their lungs, and high blood pressure. What do you do first?

options.A: Slow the infusion rate, elevate the head of the bed, and notify the provider
options.B: Flush the line rapidly with a bolus of normal saline to check patency
options.C: Place the client flat on their left side and prepare for emergency intubation
options.D: Remove the IV cannula immediately and apply a cold ice pack to the limb

explanation: Classic signs of fluid overload! Slowing the fluids and sitting the patient up helps them breathe easier while you alert the doctor. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h6)

question: Why must you always inspect the tip of an IV catheter after you remove it?

options.A: To determine what gauge size was used for the infusion
options.B: To measure the exact length of the vein inside the client's arm
options.C: To ensure the catheter tip broke off completely or remained intact
options.D: To check if any blood clots formed inside the plastic tubing

explanation: Always double-check that tiny plastic tip! Ensuring it's in one piece means no broken plastic fragment floated off into the patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the correct technique for pulling out a peripheral IV catheter?

options.A: Twist the hub rapidly while pulling outward with force
options.B: Lift the tip upward quickly at a 90-degree angle
options.C: Flush the line with saline right before pulling it out
options.D: Pull it out smoothly and parallel to the skin surface

explanation: Keep it smooth! Pulling the catheter out parallel to the skin prevents it from scraping or tearing the delicate inside lining of the vein. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h7)
